when he comes to his colleagues and asks them to exercise restraint in this difficult time.
I hope the minister will be successful in his attempts in cabinet to have his colleagues exercise restraint, which in turn will be supported by all members of the government party. This leadership by the government will set an example, I suggest, to other levels of government, and would have a worth-while effect upon our economy. It would moderate inflationary tendencies, with the secondary result of having a major influence on moderating government expenditures that are prone to inflationary tendencies.
Another aspect of the budget which has caused great concern in my part of the country is the unfortunate atmosphere of confrontation that has arisen in regard to the resource industry. I find that more and more people in western Canada are concerned over the developments that have taken place in this area. There has been a very long debate on this important issue. I certainly want to lend my voice in support of what I think is the majority point of view, and to ask the government to exercise some moderation in its approach to the issue, with a view to allowing further discussion and compromise to enter the picture, instead of taking a hard line toward resources within the boundaries of the respective provinces.
I think there is room here for discussion and compromise. It would be a very unfortunate result if hard lines were drawn on each side, both by the federal government and by the provinces. The people of western Canada to whom I have spoken about this issue are anxious that some compromise be made. I lay the blame at this point in time not upon the federal government exclusively or upon the provincial government. But there is room for compromise in the positions now being taken by the parties. That is why I hope there will be meaningful discussion and negotiation on the subject of taxation of resource industries.
I speak as a member representing a constituency in which are located some very important mining concerns.
I think Saskatoon can proudly be called the potash capital of Canada, if not of the world. The people of Saskatoon, Saskatchewan and the west are concerned that the policies of the federal government relating to the taxation of resources and royalties, so far as their being allowable expenses for taxation purposes, be not viewed uncompromisingly.
I should also like to make some suggestions regarding certain other aspects of the Income Tax Act. I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that certain areas of the act require serious consideration, with a view to change. There are disadvantaged people in society who need special consideration. I specifically refer to those members of our population who are deaf.
People in this unfortunate position are not given any personal exemption, as are those who are blind, or necessarily confined to bed or wheelchair throughout the entire year. It seems to me that this segment of our population requires the same consideration as those to whom I have just referred, and it is to be hoped the government will see fit in due course to place deaf people in the same cate-
gory. I hope this plea will not fall, if I may be pardoned for saying so, on deaf ears as far as the Minister of Finance is concerned.
I also note some anomalies regarding that classification of persons who are say, paraplegics or who suffer serious physical disability and who, because they are not necessarily confined to bed or a wheelchair for the whole of the year, do not fall within the category of exemptions referred to in the act. Again I suggest some special consideration be given by the minister to extending this category to include people who are demonstrably in this condition and who can provide medical proof.
I now want to turn to another aspect of taxation and tax exemption, registered retirement savings plans. Registered retirement savings plans, in my estimation, have been a worth-while endeavour. They have provided a very sound method for people who are either employed by companies or self-employed to build up a retirement fund and defer taxation on moneys over a period of time until they attain, at the latest, the age of 71, when they receive benefits in the form of a pension investment return from the amount of money accumulated over the years.
I think all members of the House are interested in trying to improve legislation if we can, and in bringing forward suggestions that improve the operation of such plans. Therefore, I would again put forward a suggestion in the hope that the minister will give it his favourable consideration. I refer to the present situation in respect of registered retirement savings plans where the option for re-investment in the time allotted under the present act and regulations restricts one to investments by way of annuity. Certainly an annuity, as has been pointed out, has a social virtue, I suppose, in providing income on retirement that is regular and secure, and an annuity can be bought on what might be called easy terms, with tax deferred money.
On the other hand, there is what I think an iniquitous feature in the annuity concept, in that an individual must use his total accumulation of cash on a one-shot purchase regardless of the condition of the market at the time of purchase.
For example, if an annuity were purchased at a time when market conditions were not favourable, the participant who invested in this manner would find himself in a rather unfortunate position as compared to the person who purchased under better market conditions.
Therefore, with the idea of trying to improve the operation of these provisions of the act in respect of registered retirement savings plans, I would suggest that consideration be given to introducing appropriate legislation, or amendments, allowing a retired individual under a registered retirement savings plan to take his lump sum and invest the same under the auspices of a bank, a trust company or, if he deems appropriate, an insurance company, with the idea of arranging his own personal system of withdrawal. The financial institutions to which I refer
February 3, 1975

are reputable and responsible institutions that can assure the investor that these are safe investments.
These financial institutions would be allowed to offer this particular form of investment on the basis of some reasonable fee commensurate with the work involved. I suggest they would have no right to the residue capital remaining at death, but that this would revert to the individual's estate. Presumably the surviving spouse could carry on with such a plan.
I suggest this particular proposal has some important social features. First, the retired individual would have more spending power and more ability to make an optimum return on investment. As a result such a person would less likely become a burden on our welfare and social services. In addition, the remaining capital residue under such a plan would stay within this country. It also seems to me that such a proposal or plan would maximize the return a retired individual might get on his investment.
It has been substantiated actuarially that a person may in fact increase his return through such methods of investment as opposed to being rather restricted as at the present time to the annuity situation, which is not an alternative but the only course open to people under the registered retirement savings plans they have now.
I submit this proposal to the Minister of Finance in the hope that, in considering possible amendments to the act or regulations in respect of registered retirement savings plans, he will pursue this suggestion and allow these people this option in respect of investments open to participants in registered retirement savings plans.
Let me conclude by simply making reference to a matter I raised in the House regarding Canada Savings Bonds, and the possibility that certain issues are not eligible investments for inclusion under registered retirement savings plans. I would ask the minister if he will, in fact, investigate the situation in respect of all issues of Canada Savings Bonds to make sure that some issues are not in fact ineligible investments, or to make sure that all issues qualify in respect of registered retirement savings plan investments.
I have been in correspondence with the minister in respect of this matter. My concern is that, of all things we have to invest in under our registered retirement savings plans, Canada Savings Bonds should be high on the priority for eligibility under this scheme. I have provided the minister with some information that has come into my hands that this may not be the case. I would simply ask that he pay some attention to this particular matter, and bring forward whatever amendments the regulations require to ensure that Canada Savings Bonds issues all fall within the eligible investment category.
To leave things on a positive note let me mention that in carrying out the duties of collecting taxes, either personal or otherwise, the minister and his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford), have large and efficient staffs involved in this process. As members of parliament we receive letters from time to
Income Tax
time complaining about treatment afforded individual taxpayers by people involved in collecting taxes. I would simply draw the minister's attention to the importance of treating these people who are involved with these departments with courtesy and attention.
It is hoped that from time to time the appropriate ministers will, by way of directive, remind public servants that they are in fact exactly that, public servants, and should exercise to the best of their ability courtesy when dealing with people who approach them. They should understand that very often people are not familiar with the complexities of taxation. They should keep in mind that the number of changes has been incredible. The size of this bill alone would testify to the fact that the changes to the Income Tax Act are many.
Let me suggest to the minister that he should from time to time in his wisdom remind public servants that the average citizen is anxious to do the right thing in respect of his tax return, and is very often anxious to obtain information. A courteous reception would be very much appreciated. I know that 99.9 per cent of tax employees are kind and efficient, but I think it bears repeating, because we get these complaints from time to time, that this point should be brought to the attention of departmental officials.

Madam Speaker, for the government, Bill C-49 is one of the most important of all the bills introduced in the current session, because its purpose is to bring revenue to the treasury. That is the concern of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). His main function is to bring in the income the government requires to enable the ministers of the cabinet and the departments to function and manage the affairs of the country. That is his main responsibility.
I congratulate him for championing Bill C-49 with such vigour.
He is certainly sincere and convinced of the need for his bill, but I doubt very much that he is convinced that all Canadian taxpayers will be pleased with it, especially in the present context in which we live, where every taxpayer is extremely concerned about the income he wants and needs, depending on the size of his family, to meet his obligations.
Now, his bill is quite voluminous, Madam Speaker. That aspect has always struck me in this House. When we set about getting money out of the pockets of the taxpayers, we always get bills that are heavy, that can be measured, not in centimeters or millimeters, but in inches, our current unit measure. Remember the bill of 1971, the so-called tax reform bill: that was a three-inch brick. At that time, we had advised the Canadian taxpayers of the results of that bill on their income, of the taxes they would have to pay, as we had also warned the small businesses about the taxes they would have to pay as a result of that bill.
I remember how, at that time, we had managed to arouse the attention of a certain segment of the population, though not enough to prevent the then Minister of

February 3, 1975
Income Tax
Finance from having the bill passed, that is the tax reform.
Yet, Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance

an intelligent man, I admit-predicts that 1975 will be an extremely difficult year for Canada. I do not know if this is due to the fact that our southern neighbours foresee great difficulties in their own country. And I refer to the news of yesterday and the day before on Canadian television to the effect that the President of the United States foresees a deficit of $52 billion, not million, but $52 billion. Now that is a deficit!
Since we are live side by side, it is obvious that if our neighbour has the flu or a virus, there is much danger, since we are so close, that we shall catch the same virus, and I believe that we have caught it. We are also affected by this economic fever virus. According to previsions, 1975 will be an extremely difficult year. But why should this year be more difficult than 1974? This is what we should ask ourselves as parliamentarians, as people responsible for giving to the country and administration of which the taxpayers will be satisfied and which would allow development and progress in our country and which would give workers the possibility of living better, of being in a better financial situation than at the end of 1975.
What do we have to fear, Madam Speaker? We are not God. We cannot guess whether there will be a ca-tastrophy. We cannot guess whether there will be a drought or a flood. We have to leave this to the Divine Providence. If this were up to men, I believe that the situation would be worse than it has been up till now.
What do we have to fear? Will there be a shortage of workers to build housing for Canadians? Will there be a shortage of raw materials for producing what Canadians need to fill their daily needs, such as housing, food, medical and hospital services, and road services to go from place to place? But then, what have we to fear if all the Cabinet ministers do their duties, if the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) plays his role, which is to introduce social legislation ensuring all Canadians a guaranteed minimum income, medical care and housing?
He is responsible for the well-being of Canadians. Another minister, who is responsible for housing, who must ensure that Canadians have a decent house, announced last week the introduction of a piece of legislation inviting all Canadians, through provincial and municipal governments, to use every possible means to ensure decent housing for each Canadian, each family.
So another minister who is determined to do his duty.
I also heard in this House the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) say in a most eloquent way to the people of this country that in the area of transportation his department will be efficient, that they will do everything possible to ensure that all areas-
Hear, hear.

I commend you for applauding him.
[Mr. Lambert (Bellechasse) J

speechtext: Order. Ask the labour unions why they have strikes? It is to get more money for their membership, and especially for labour leaders. We have seen that. Ask those who own a business why they need money. It is to have a higher income. Bill C-49 says: an Act to amend the statute law relating to income tax. So the Minister of Finance-and through no fault of his-is instructed under our constitution to dip into the incomes of people. I am considering, Madam Speaker, whether the people are really being treated fairly, if this bill really gives them adequate exemptions, or whether, on the other hand, they are being taxed too heavily compared to the income they can make in 1975. Indeed, Madam Speaker, I think that it is perfectly in order for me to reason thus because if one must restrict oneself to dollars and cents, one can read from page to page. But I am afraid we shall not succeed in suggesting to the minister intelligent amendments which would be likely to help him apply the tax legislation in a universally just and fair way.
It is with this in mind that I intend to consider Bill C-49. If I am not mistaken, the bill has now reached second reading. It is therefore the gist of the bill we must be concerned about. I am considering the principles of this bill and trying, with all the open-mindedness which can be expected from an hon. member, to deal exclusively with the very principle on which this bill is based. Then, I am trying all sorts of explanations in support of my views, in order to convey them to my hon. colleagues in the House and especially the Minister of Finance. In other words, if we must adopt this bill without having the opportunity to deal with it honestly and intelligently, I wonder why we are here. We should merely let the minister introduce his bill to the cabinet and the matter would be settled. Well, Madam Speaker, I feel it is our duty to vindicate the fundamental rights of individuals, the fundamental rights and responsibilities of Canadian taxpayers, for I have never been able to understand how, in a well organized society, individuals could have only responsibilities.
I never wanted to accept that. I understand we all have rights, but we also have commitments. I wish those commitments, which every Canadian shares in, would match their capacities in contributing, for the common welfare, to the payment of those expenditures which the govern-
February 3, 1975

ment has to incur to enforce some act or other, to secure every Canadian's well-being.
Madam Speaker, if you allow me to proceed with my statement, I would like to demonstrate that we, in Canada, really face an extremely serious situation. I receive daily from my constituents numerous requests for information respecting Canada's housing legislation. In other words, there are people in our country who live in unsatisfactory conditions and would like to take advantage of the legislation. They come and tell me: I heard on the radio that a bill was introduced, and another one passed. But people know nothing of their content. So they ask me for information, just as they ask the hon. member for Riviere-du-Loup-Temiscouata (Mr. Gendron) here in front of me, and every member of this House in order to be able to take advantage of those acts.
I also receive numerous requests daily from people who want to work. They do not want to be unemployed, they want to earn a living, they want to work on construction projects, either in the building of houses or in the development of resources, in the James Bay area for instance. Madam Speaker, I have seen with my own eyes lines of workers queueing up in front of employment offices, wanting jobs in the James Bay area, to develop our natural resources, develop the energy we need in Canada. All those people apply at their Manpower Centers. They also call on their members of Parliament, anxious to take advantage of a certain influence which will enable them to sell their work to develop resources in Canada and take part, through their work and their efforts, in the development and gross national production of Canada.
Madam Speaker, I personally heard the minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), on a news report, say "that he fears Canada's gross national out-put will slow down in 1975". Why would there be a slow-down? Why would that be when Canadians are ready to do more. Why are our standard of living and our social security acts linked to the Gross National Product?
Madam Speaker, if our GNP is lower in 1975 than in 1974, there is a reason for it, there may even be a number of reasons. This, in my view, explains the dangerous path our country is following. We are going down the drain. Unemployment brings inflation. Inflation breeds unemployment. And unemployment and inflation breed scarce money.
The artificial scarcity of money we are now facing causes interest rate hikes. And when interest rates go up, there is no incentive to go ahead, to create a new industry, to provide jobs, to produce more, to raise the GNP. The capable people, companies or individuals, are stopped in their tracks because interest rates are too high. They don't understand and get discouraged.
Madam Speaker, I believe we are now debating the most important bill in this session, because the success or failure of our whole Canadian economy depends on it.
I would like my remarks to be as clear as possible. I would like to show once and for all that policies used until now are not adequate, not in keeping with our objecive. Madam Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock.

subtopic: COPYRIGHT ACT-SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO PROTECT AUTHORS AGAINST IMPORTED EDITIONS OF THEIR BOOKS
COPYRIGHT ACT-SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO PROTECT AUTHORS AGAINST IMPORTED EDITIONS OF THEIR BOOKS
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I recognize the solemnity of the occasion, it being one week after Robbie Burns day.
I had hoped the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) would have been in the House when I raised my question this afternoon but I note he was called out, presumably on urgent public business.
While responsibility for the Copyright Act is the jurisdiction of his colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), I believe the subject matter of my inquiry is of the greatest possible concern to the Secretary of State.
An interest in preserving our cultural and literary heritage must be one of the chief priorities of his portfolio. I will believe he is taking these responsibilities seriously-until his extended tenure in office proves me wrong. I hope, therefore, that he will be seized of the importance of the matter which I have raised and which was raised initially and most perceptively by Mr. McClelland and two Canadian authors, Farley Mowat and Pierre Berton, about ten days ago.
McClelland and Stewart have been in the very forefront of those who took the risk-and not so long ago it was a risk-of publishing Canadian authors on Canadian topics. The views of Mr. McClelland deserve respect and consideration from anyone interested in the future of Canadian authors and publishers.
The press release of January 22, which I commend to the minister and all members, sets out the case with real cogency. By importing overstocks, remainders and regular foreign editions of works by Canadian authors some concerns have deprived these authors of rightful income, and of course have injured the Canadian publishers who in the first instance brought these works forward to the Canadian reading public.
It little profits that we make a mighty roar of trumpets over what is to be done to Time and Reader's Digest if, at the same time, we allow a provision in another Canadian statute to injure creative Canadian writers.
Putting it in simplistic terms, we have a situation whereunder American publishers of the works of Canadian authors are dumping lower priced editions on the Canadian market. This is not being done by the American publishers directly but by jobbers, wholesalers and remainder houses.
The matter is not just a case of loss of revenue by people like Pierre Berton and Farley Mowat, although that is regrettable enough-whether we like their view of the north and the CTR is a matter of indifference.
February 3, 1975

Adjournment Debate
Rather it is a problem of diminishing or curtailing the production of Canadian publishing houses. For instance, McClelland and Stewart have been forced to abandon publication of their planned paperback editions of Mowat works. It is not hard to realize the injurious effect of this sort of shrinkage as the competition from cheaper American editions of Canadian works becomes more and more pervasive.
The press statement of January 22 points to section 28 of the Copyright Act as the problem area. The Copyright Act is a complex statute doubtless in need of careful study, reappraisal, and possibly substantial amendment. Such a process on a statute of this kind with international complications may take as long as two years. But the Canadian publishing industry cannot wait that long. Too many Canadian authors-both the great and the lowly-will suffer.
It is therefore of the essence that an early move to amend section 28 be initiated. I would commend to the minister a course of those usual consultations among party representatives so that quick passage may be achieved, and quick remedial action on this grave problem undertaken.
We cannot always parade our intellectual nationalism in great battalions. Often we preserve our cultural identity by important but mundane moves to check recognized chinks in our nationalist defences. The Copyright Act may not seem a glamorous badge of Canadianism, but the removal of the iniquity in section 28 could be many times more efficacious than a hundred after dinner speeches or the flutterings of a thousand Maple Leaf flags. I urge the minister to prompt action, and pledge him and his colleagues in the government my full support.

subtopic: ENERGY-REQUEST FOR CANCELLATION OF SALE OF CANDU REACTOR TO ARGENTINA-SUGGESTION NO FURTHER SALES BE MADE IN VIEW OF LACK OF SAFEGUARDS
ENERGY-REQUEST FOR CANCELLATION OF SALE OF CANDU REACTOR TO ARGENTINA-SUGGESTION NO FURTHER SALES BE MADE IN VIEW OF LACK OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on November 28 last I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to consider cancelling the sale of a CANDU reactor to Argentina on the grounds that we were seeking safeguards from a country which is dominated by a highly volatile political situation. At that time I also tried to point out to the Prime Minister that there are no safeguards; that, as a matter of fact, the only real safeguard is, "no sale".
Let me quote from Thomas Perry's "Nuclear Energy in Canada-Potential and Problems", as printed in "Nature Canada." He wrote:
Opponents of fission energy point out a number of differences between the real world and the 'technological paradise'. Fission energy is safe only if a number of critical devices work as they should-if a number of people in key positions follow all their instructions, if there is no sabotage, no hijacking of the transports, if no reactor fuel processing plant or repository anywhere in the world is situated in a region of riots or guerrilla activity, and no revolution or war-even a 'conventional' one-takes place in these regions.
The enormous quantities of extremely dangerous material must not get into the hands of ignorant people or desperados. No acts of God can be permitted.
Even if there were such things as safeguards, Canada seems to seek customers in areas that fly in the face of the most optimistic proponents of CANDU sales. Our most recent customers are Argentina, a country marked by political turmoil since World War II and becoming increasingly more volatile, and South Korea, a region wracked by internal civil war, oppression and political assassination. It is not as though we did not have the experience of India. It is not as though we have not witnessed the fallibility of the wisdom of our leaders.
We can try to cover up what happened in India, but the fact of the matter is that we sold India a CANDU reactor; we sought safeguards; they gave us safeguards; the Canadian government then said that the safeguards were adequate; yet India used our technology and produced a nuclear explosion. We can look at India and say we had inadequate safeguards; but on December 20, 1974, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) stood up in the House and said as recorded at page 2429 of Hansard:
I would like now to outline the provisions that will be required in every safeguards arrangement. The provisions, to be administered by the International Atomic Energy Agency, or through appropriate alternative procedures meeting the requirements of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of nuclear Weapons, will cover all nuclear facilities and equipment supplied by Canada for the life of those facilities and equipment.
Specifically, these safeguards sound impressive. However, it is spine chilling to note that these also have inherent weaknesses. It should be pointed out that the International Atomic Energy Agency differentiates between military and peaceful nuclear devices, while Canada does not. The nuclear non-proliferation treaty received much fanfare when it was signed, but several important countries refused to sign. Among them are
February 3, 1975

India, Argentina and South Korea. Furthermore, India and Argentina have already signed a nuclear technology exchange agreement. Argentina can easily learn all it may want to know about nuclear weaponry from India, regardless of the faith Canada has in its mythical safeguards.
Who is our next customer? My information tells me that our busy little CANDU salesmen have packed then-bags full of nuclear goodies and are marching to Pretoria-yes, Madam Speaker-South Africa!
In my two years as a member of this House I have accused the government of incompetence, as in the transportation mess. I have accused it of regional insensitivity. I have accused it of a lack of social concern in the matters of unemployment and old age pensions. However, in this instance of fooling around with nuclear capability, I am beginning to suspect that this cabinet is as looney as a bunch of bedbugs.
On November 28 last the Prime Minister went on to tell me that to take my attitude of wanting to ban CANDU sales would mean that Canada would sit on this very advanced technology and not be willing to share even its benefits with some countries of the world that do not have our advantages;-I would add, Madam Speaker, also-our disadvantages. One of the disadvantages is the management of radio-active wastes. Today's nuclear reactors are producing over 13,000 pounds of plutonium per year, and the rate of production will continue to rise. By 1977 it will be 40,000 pounds annually, and by 1982 over 220,000 pounds annually.
Plutonium is regarded by scientists as the most dangerous substance known to man. It is extremely toxic and radio-active-one thousandth of one gram of plutonium is all that is necessary to snuff out one life. Twenty-two pounds will build an atomic bomb. If these facts are not frightening enough, let me point out that scientists warn that radio isotope plutonium 239, significantly found in the waste of conventional fission reactors, must be isolated from man's environment for 488,000 years.
Scientists tell us further that Canadian waste management measures have only been temporary to date and no large-scale reprocessing has taken place. A fine legacy for our children! Therefore, what technology would we be withholding? We sell them hope for today, with no assurance that there will be a tomorrow.
The truth is that we are out to sell the CANDU reactor to whichever countries have the cash and want to buy. We even have on the spot financing through the Export Development Corporation for those countries which do not have $600 million ready cash. I can repeat what Walter Stewart has warned, when we are off selling the CANDU willy-nilly for the bucks, we should remember that all sales could be final.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-REQUEST FOR CANCELLATION OF SALE OF CANDU REACTOR TO ARGENTINA-SUGGESTION NO FURTHER SALES BE MADE IN VIEW OF LACK OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a great pleasure to be able to respond to the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) on
Adjournment Debate
this question concerning safeguards on the sale of a CANDU reactor to Argentina.
Argentina concluded a safeguards agreement with the International Atomic Energy Agency. This agreement meets in full the requirements of the IAEA. Furthermore, Argentina has given formal assurances to Canada that the exports contemplated under the sale of designated Canadian equipment, material and technology would be used only for peaceful purposes and would not be used for the development of any nuclear explosive device. In addition, negotiations are nearing completion on a bilateral agreement between Canada and Argentina meeting the specific safeguards requirements outlined by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) on December 20, 1974.
Canada considers that it has a responsibility to participate in efforts to solve the world's energy problems and wishes to use its nuclear technology to help in gaining this objective. It will do so, however, only on the basis of the most stringent safeguards to ensure that Canada's nuclear exports are devoted solely to peaceful nonexplosive purposes.

subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-BRITISH COLUMBIA-ESCAPE OF TWO INMATES-SUGGESTED MANNING OF TOWERS TWENTY-FOUR HOURS A DAY
PENITENTIARIES-BRITISH COLUMBIA-ESCAPE OF TWO INMATES-SUGGESTED MANNING OF TOWERS TWENTY-FOUR HOURS A DAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on October 9, 1974, I asked the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) when he was going to man the towers of the British Columbia penitentiary again, because they had discontinued manning the towers some time previously. The Solicitor General replied that they had manned the towers when they had had difficulties with security, but now they did not feel the need was there any longer.
On December 10, two months later, I once more had to ask the Solicitor General the same question, because in the meantime, in the first week of December, two very dangerous criminals had escaped from the British Columbia penitentiary and caused great concern to the people on the lower mainland of British Columbia. I am sad to say that the towers are still not manned in the British Columbia penitentiary, and that the need is still there.
The Solicitor General in his last answer talked of the cost of manning the towers and the fact that the escape rate had dropped by 50 per cent over the previous year. But two escapes have brought that percentage up to the rate in the previous year.
I ask, at what time would inmates escape from a penitentiary? During the daytime the complement of security guards inside the penitentiary is four times what it is at night. There are no guards in the towers at night, which makes it easier for people who go outside the penitentiary before lock-up to stay outside.
The Solicitor General talked about the cost of manning the towers. I am wondering what the cost of recapturing the criminals who escaped was. It would be very hard to get an exact figure from anybody of what it cost to bring back these two dangerous criminals, but there was a police alert, and the police worked overtime. So far as

February 3, 1975
Adjournment Debate
costs are concerned, we are talking only of four men on the night shift, and minimum salaries in the penitentiary are around $7,500 a year. In other words, we are looking at a cost of about $30,000 a year to man four towers, which would give us much more security in the area and would possibly stop these dangerous escapes.
I am sorry to see that neither the Solicitor General nor the parliamentary secretary is here tonight to tell the people who live in this area that these two towers are going to be manned. These people are quite concerned about the situation. I was in the area the other night and I could see the lights on outside, but the towers were still empty. This is a maximum security penitentiary, and the towers should be manned. I do not think the Solicitor General can use the excuse of cost, because the cost is minimal compared to the cost of recapturing escaped criminals. I hope that very shortly the Solicitor General will be able to tell the House that the towers will be manned once again.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Foster (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-BRITISH COLUMBIA-ESCAPE OF TWO INMATES-SUGGESTED MANNING OF TOWERS TWENTY-FOUR HOURS A DAY
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I should like to give the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) some information supplied to me by the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), who is unable to be here this evening, concerning his question about the manning of the towers at the B.C. penitentiary.
First of all, I should like to refer to the escape mentioned by the hon. member in his question in the House in December. During the evening of the escape incident there were two musical performances scheduled to be given by an outside group at the penitentiary as a pre-Christmas recreational activity. Since the gymnasium cannot accommodate the total inmate population at one time, the group had to perform twice during the evening, with half the inmate population attending each performance.
On completion of the performance, the half of the population then in attendance returned to their respective cells while the second half of the population was admitted to the gymnasium. In a routine manner, the first group of inmates returned to their cells, and their beds.
The correctional officers, on completion of the evening recreational period and the return of the inmates to their cells at 11 p.m., took the regular inmate count. Seeing that some inmates were apparently asleep in their beds,
they did not disturb these inmates during the counting procedures and counted those bodies which they believed they saw.
One of the inmates involved in the escape was a member of the gymnasium maintenance crew, a position which permitted him access to the recreational facility on a daily basis under the supervision of a recreational officer. It appears that, over a period of time, he prepared the escape route under the gymnasium stage, where he managed to stash the contraband articles required for the escape.
Before attending the Christmas concert the two inmates placed well-disguised, body-like paraphernalia in their beds. These disguises were complete with shoes, and earphones covering face masks, covered by a blanket on the beds. After leaving their respective cells for the gymnasium, they crawled unobserved under the stage and made good their escape from the gymnasium at around midnight. They had hoped the officers taking the routine inmate count would take the disguises left in the beds for sleeping inmates, and not disturb inmates who had already gone to sleep.
Once the count had been made and everyone apparently accounted for, the officers manning the towers were taken off their posts. The institution at this point continued to be subject to security coverage by a one-man inside yard patrol, a one-man mobilized perimeter wall control, and the regular night shift security staff.
With regard to the question of manning the towers, I would like to inform the hon. member that the patrol in the interior yard was increased during those hours when the towers were no longer being manned. It is not considered necessary to have the towers manned during the hours after midnight when the inmates are locked in their cells, in view of these extra precautions. The practice of manning the towers was put into effect for a trial period last year. However, it was deemed unnecessary and too expensive.
I trust that the forgoing information will be of assistance to the hon. member.

The motion to adjourn the House is now deemed to have been adopted. Accordingly, this House stands adjourned until tomorrow at 2 p.m.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.24 p.m.

Tuesday, February 4, 1975
